numberItems.stem: Compared with running empty, how does a full load change a combination's rollover risk in a crash?
options: It makes a rollover 5 times more likely
It makes a rollover 10 times more likely
It makes a rollover less likely because the rig is heavier
numberItems.explanation: Fully loaded rigs are 10 times more likely to roll over in an accident than empty rigs. Some websites say 5 times; the handbook says 10 (p. 6-1).

numberItems.stem: Which is one of the two things the handbook says will help you prevent a rollover?
options: Load the heaviest cargo on top so it holds the load down
Drive slowly around turns
Change lanes quickly to spend less time in curves
numberItems.explanation: Two things help prevent rollover: keep the cargo as close to the ground as possible, and drive slowly around turns (p. 6-1).

options: In a quick lane change, the trailer swings much harder than the tractor and can turn over
In a turn, the rear wheels follow a path inside the front wheels
The tractor jackknifes when its drive wheels lock
numberItems.explanation: Trucks with trailers have a crack-the-whip effect: a quick lane change can turn the trailer over, and in many crashes only the trailer overturns (p. 6-1).

numberItems.stem: In Figure 6.1, which rig has the lowest rearward amplification — the least crack-the-whip effect?
options: Triple 27-ft trailers
65-ft conventional double with 27-ft trailers
5-axle tractor-semitrailer with a 45-ft trailer
numberItems.explanation: Figure 6.1 lists rigs from least to most crack-the-whip; the 5-axle tractor-semitrailer with a 45-ft trailer is at the top (p. 6-2).

numberItems.stem: A rearward amplification of **2.0** means the rear trailer is:
options: 3.5 times as likely to turn over as the tractor
Twice as likely to turn over as the tractor
10 times as likely to turn over as the tractor
numberItems.explanation: Rearward amplification of 2.0 means the rear trailer is twice as likely to turn over as the tractor (p. 6-1).

numberItems.stem: According to Figure 6.1, triples with 27-ft trailers have a rearward amplification of:
numberItems.explanation: Triples have a rearward amplification of 3.5 — you can roll the last trailer 3.5 times as easily as a 5-axle tractor (p. 6-1).

numberItems.stem: What is the handbook's minimum following-distance rule for combination vehicles?
options: At least 2 seconds for each 10 feet of vehicle length
At least 1 second for each 10 feet of length, plus 1 more second at 40 mph or below
At least 1 second for each 10 feet of length, plus 1 more second when going over 40 mph
numberItems.explanation: Follow at least 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length, plus another second if going over 40 mph (p. 6-1).

numberItems.stem: Which combination takes longer to stop?
options: An empty combination
A fully loaded combination
They stop in about the same distance
numberItems.explanation: Large combinations take longer to stop when empty: stiff springs and strong brakes give poor traction and the wheels lock easily (p. 6-2).

numberItems.stem: Your rig is stuck on a railroad crossing. You are out and away from the tracks. What should you especially give when you call 9-1-1?
options: Your CDL number
The crossing's DOT number, if posted
Your trailer's license plate number
numberItems.explanation: Give the location of the crossing using all identifiable landmarks, especially the DOT number, if posted (p. 6-2).

options: The trailer's wheels lock up and the trailer swings around
The trailer tips over in a quick lane change
The tractor's drive wheels spin on ice
numberItems.explanation: When the trailer wheels lock up, the trailer tends to swing around — a trailer jackknife, more likely when empty or lightly loaded (p. 6-3).

options: The trailer drifting off course while you back up
The trailer swinging out during a quick lane change
In a turn, the rear wheels following a different path than the front wheels
numberItems.explanation: When a vehicle goes around a corner, the rear wheels follow a different path than the front wheels — off-tracking or "cheating" (p. 6-3).

numberItems.stem: You can't finish a right turn without entering another lane. Which method does the handbook call correct?
options: Swing wide to the left before starting the turn (jug handle)
Turn wide as you complete the turn (button hook)
Keep the rear of the rig well away from the curb
numberItems.explanation: Turn wide as you complete the turn (button hook); swinging left first (jug handle) lets drivers pass you on the right. Keep the rear close to the curb (pp. 6-3–6-4).

numberItems.stem: You are backing a tractor-trailer and want the trailer to go **right**. Which way do you turn the top of the steering wheel?
options: To the left
To the right
Keep it straight
numberItems.explanation: When backing a trailer, turn the wheel in the opposite direction: top of the wheel left makes the trailer go right (p. 6-4).

numberItems.stem: [CA] Are triple trailers legal to pull in California?
options: Yes, with a "T" endorsement
Yes, but only on freeways
No — triple trailers are not legal in California
numberItems.explanation: The handbook states: "Triple trailers are not legal in California" (p. 1-5).
